summary.text: Take the admissible even value \(m=10\). The bound \(q\le \lfloor 10/4\rfloor=2\) forces the prime \(q=2\), hence \(p=10-q=8\), which is not prime; thus no required representation exists, independently of the Jacobi condition.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the refinement by exhibiting an admissible even integer for which the required representation cannot exist. Take
\[
m=10.
\]
This integer satisfies all the hypotheses in the even part of the conjecture: it is even, it is greater than \(8\), and it is neither \(32\) nor \(152\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that the claimed even refinement holds for \(m=10\). Then there must exist primes \(p\) and \(q\) such that
\[
10=p+q,
\]
with
\[
q\leq \frac{10}{4},
\]
where the quotient is the integer quotient appearing in the conjecture. Thus
\[
q\leq \left\lfloor\frac{10}{4}\right\rfloor=2.
\]
On the other hand, every prime natural number is at least \(2\). Since \(q\) is prime, we therefore have \(q\geq 2\). Combining this with \(q\leq 2\) gives
\[
q=2.
\]
Substituting this into the required equation \(10=p+q\) yields
\[
10=p+2,
\]
and hence
\[
p=8.
\]
But \(8\) is not prime, since \(8=2\cdot4\). This contradicts the requirement that \(p\) be prime.

Consequently, no pair of primes \(p,q\) can satisfy even the additive equation and size bound required by the refinement at \(m=10\). In particular, there cannot be such a pair also satisfying the additional Jacobi-symbol condition
\[
\left(\frac{(q+1)/2}{r}\right)=1
\quad\text{for every prime divisor }r\mid 11.
\]
The Jacobi condition therefore requires no separate analysis: the necessary prime representation already does not exist.

Thus \(10\) is an even integer greater than \(8\), outside the stated exceptional set \(\{32,152\}\), for which the conjectured representation is impossible. Hence the even clause is false, and therefore the conjunction of the odd and even clauses in Sun's refinement conjecture is false.
